messages.subject: MRDS where some transects only have a single observer
messages.subject_clean: MRDS where some transects only have a single observer
messages.body_plain:
I'm currently doing an analysis of some mark-recapture distance sampling data for an arboreal mammal. The majority of transects were surveyed by two observers working independently. For these transects it has been straightforward to fit a MRDS model ( point independence variant) using the mrds package in R, with code like this:

ddf.hr <http://ddf.hr><-ddf(method="io",
            dsmodel=~cds(key="hr", adj.series=NULL, adj.order=NULL, formula=~1),
            mrmodel=~glm(link="logit", formula=~distance),
            data=detections,
            meta.data=meta)

Where  detections is a dataframe containing the distance data (2 entries for each animal recording detection or not by observer 1 and 2), and meta is the list of metadata settings for the model fitting process (not shown here). So far, so good. The model works well, and presented no particular difficulties.

My question is, whether there is a way to incorporate data from some additional transects that were surveyed using the same methods, but only by a single observer. My thinking here is that if the detection process on these transects is equivalent to that for the first observer on a double-observer transect, then such a model should be estimable. However adding single-observer entries to the detections data.frame for animals observed on the single-observer transects (which usually contains two rows for each individual animal recording detection or not by each observer) results in an error message:

Error in process.data(data, meta.data) :
  number of records for primary observer not equal to number for secondary observer

Is there perhaps a way to trick mrds into estimating the model I have in mind? Or is this either a very bad idea, or something that is not possible for mrds to do?

Regards,

Michael Scroggie

messages.subject_clean: DSM and stratification by region (habitat)
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have a few questions about stratification in distance sampling and dsm, and would appreciate community input.

Opening statements:
1. "Stratification can be used to increase the precision of estimates if we know a priori that density varies between different parts of the study area. As an example, the minke whale data contain two strata: North and South relating to strata further away from and nearer to the Antarctic ice edge, respectively." (Miller et al. 2019 doi: 10.18637/jss.v089.i01).

2. "In design-based sampling, unequal sampling intensity is often accommodated via stratification" (Conn et al. 2017 MEE).

3. (Taken from the minke whale example R script): " When a detection function is fitted to data pooled across strata, the results are actually incorrect because effort was not equally allocated between the strata. The southern stratum is much smaller (84000km2) than the northern (630000km2). But the southern stratum is more desirable habitat for the minke whales.  The southern stratum had much greater survey effort per area than the northern stratum. This is not represented in the pooled analysis."

Now some questions. Say I want to fit a dsm to the Minke Whale data. My main questions is: "Can I use stratification in (the steps of) a dsm to increase precision?"

Q1. Is it correct that stratification of the study region will influence the results of the dsm IF stratum is fitted as a covariate in the detection function AND detection varies by stratum? I think it will, as covariates in the detection function are included in the fitted spatial model as an offset to the count (Miller et al 2013).

Q2. True or false: Stratification will ONLY influence the dsm if detection probability varies by stratum. If detection probability is the same across strata (and thus not included in the detection function) then stratification will not influence the dsm (even if animal densities vary between strata).

Let's put it all together:
Q3. Assume I want to fit a dsm to minke whale data where: (1) animal densities vary by strata (strata is defined by 3 levels of ice concentration) (2) I have unequal sampling coverage between these strata (3) I have a detection function with equal detection between strata (either because detection function tests indicated this (*opposite to the simulated Minke example data*), or because I have to assume so based on constraints (e.g., too few detections in some strata)).

My own attempt to answer Q3: The dsm itself will not incorporate ''stratification'' in the traditional sense (stratification will not be applicable to increase the precision of estimates, but we expect increased uncertainty where there is low sampling effort). But a dsm is appropriate because "In some sense DSM is a post-stratification, but in the sense that you are explicitly modelling how density changes as a function of the covariates (here ice concentration that would define strata), rather than defining areas over which to estimate density." (copied from one of Dave Miller's answers ("DSM and stratification by year").

Thanks in advance for your confirmation/correction/answers on the above questions/statements.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Apologies if I am over-simplifying, but would there be any disadvantage to treating all observer input as independent transects? Granted, the areas being sampled by each of the paired observers overlaps, but this shouldn't matter either for estimating the detection function (the more data the merrier!) or, provided effort is specified correctly, estimating density. And there should be no problem in adding in data from single observer transects. The only reason I can think of for not doing this is if detection efficiency of an observer in a paired transect is materially affected by the presence of their partner observer (e.g. if there is communication between them to during the transect that leads to more animals being detected than would otherwise be the case; or if animals flushed from one transect are sometimes picked up by the observer on the other transect). If there are differences in efficiency between individual observers, I'd have thought this could be accounted for by including observer ID in the model.

Cheers,

Mark

Hi Mark,

Thanks for your suggestion, but I don't think that would work in our case, because g(0) is substantially less than one. The purpose for using the two observers in our surveys is to gather independent detection data for animals along the transect from two observers, and use a mark-recapture component of the model to infer g(0), thereby correcting for non-detection of animals on the line. Of course, if g(0)=1, then you can just treat the two observers as extra effort as you suggested.

Regards,

Michael Scroggie

Hi Michael, hi listfolks,

Interesting question, which I think distills down to: "can I use
multiple detection functions of different types to obtain one abundance
estimate?"

Eric is correct that there's currently no way in mrds/Distance to do
this unfortunately. I'd like to eventually add to mrds/Distance the
ability to build this kind of joint model.

In the meantime I wonder if a simplistic "manual" version of the
functionality I was thinking about would work. At the moment you have an
estimate of abundance from your MRDS study. You could fit a separate
detection function to the single observer observations and then post-hoc
correct them for g(0), assuming the same value that you got in your MRDS
analysis, then average the densities over the two separate analyses
(you'd assume independence and the CV^2 would add). This would make
sense if there were plenty of single observer observations, but if you
don't have many then the detection function and encounter rate
uncertainties for the single observer bit would end up being rather large.

I can think of more advanced versions of the above but they are rather
more involved and might not be worth it if you don't have that many more
observations or are uncomfortable applying the g(0) estimate to these
other observations.

cheers,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris, hi listfolk,

For a standard, non-spatial line transect survey, it's often the case
that stratification is recommended to reduce variance. But that variance
reduction comes mostly from a reduction in the encounter rate
uncertainty. I say this because usually encounter rate uncertainty is
larger than detection function uncertainty in line transects and the
driving force in the encounter rate variance is the between-transect
differences. Stratifying tries to put similar transects together (in the
  minke example based on high/low density areas), making the per-stratum
variance smaller.

For a density surface model, we have effectively substituted-in the
spatial model in place of the encounter rate variance. This tends to
reduce variance as we're taking into account variation over the whole
study area as a function of environmental covariates (in some sense
taking the continuous version of stratification).

Instead of thinking "stratum covariate in the detection function" we
might be better thinking of this as any other covariate that varies at
the segment level (e.g., Beaufort, wind speed, etc). In this case we can
reduce the detection function variance by including the covariate
(assuming the covariate does explain something about detectability, of
course). This will have the knock-on of reducing the total variance in
your final estimates.

I guess I'd wonder if you have "better" detection covariates than
stratum (which tend to be big) which might have a bigger effect on the
variance (like sighting conditions).

Finally, to your questions:

1. Yes, including a covariate in the detection function will have some
effect on the resulting DSM. What that effect is depends on the
covariate you add, the survey details etc, of course.

2. If detectability is constant, you don't see the effect. I'm not 100%
sure what you mean by "stratification" if there is no covariate in the
detection function. One could include "stratum" in formula for the
spatial model, this would account for density changes (coarsely), which
may be of interest.

3. No question in this one but I'll run with it. Yes, I think your
analysis is correct. As I said above, if you think of your ice
concentration "strata" as an ice concentration covariate, you might find
that this will affect the detectability (more ice==harder to see minkes)
which would be fine as a detection function covariate. Alternatively it
might not be useful and you have a detection function with no/other
covariates. Also fine. The DSM sorts out the unequal coverage issue and
the spatial density changes through the spatial model.

Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave

> Hi everyone,
>
> I have a few questions about stratification in distance sampling and
> dsm, and would appreciate community input.
>
> Opening statements:
> 1. "Stratification can be used to increase the precision of estimates if
> we know a priori that density varies between different parts of the
> study area. As an example, the minke whale data contain two strata:
> North and South relating to strata further away from and nearer to the
> Antarctic ice edge, respectively." (Miller et al. 2019 doi:
> 10.18637/jss.v089.i01).
>
> 2. "In design-based sampling, unequal sampling intensity is often
> accommodated via stratification" (Conn et al. 2017 MEE).
>
> 3. (Taken from the minke whale example R script): " When a detection
> function is fitted to data pooled across strata, the results are
> actually incorrect because effort was not equally allocated between the
> strata. The southern stratum is much smaller (84000km2) than the
> northern (630000km2). But the southern stratum is more desirable habitat
> for the minke whales.  The southern stratum had much greater survey
> effort per area than the northern stratum. This is not represented in
> the pooled analysis."
>
> Now some questions. Say I want to fit a dsm to the Minke Whale data. My
> main questions is: "Can I use stratification in (the steps of) a dsm to
> increase precision?"
>
> Q1. Is it correct that stratification of the study region will influence
> the results of the dsm IF stratum is fitted as a covariate in the
> detection function AND detection varies by stratum? I think it will, as
> covariates in the detection function are included in the fitted spatial
> model as an offset to the count (Miller et al 2013).
>
> Q2. True or false: Stratification will ONLY influence the dsm if
> detection probability varies by stratum. If detection probability is the
> same across strata (and thus not included in the detection function)
> then stratification will not influence the dsm (even if animal densities
> vary between strata).
>
> Let's put it all together:
> Q3. Assume I want to fit a dsm to minke whale data where: (1) animal
> densities vary by strata (strata is defined by 3 levels of ice
> concentration) (2) I have unequal sampling coverage between these strata
> (3) I have a detection function with equal detection between strata
> (either because detection function tests indicated this (*opposite to
> the simulated Minke example data*), or because I have to assume so based
> on constraints (e.g., too few detections in some strata)).
>
> My own attempt to answer Q3: The dsm itself will not incorporate
> ''stratification'' in the traditional sense (stratification will not be
> applicable to increase the precision of estimates, but we expect
> increased uncertainty where there is low sampling effort). But a dsm is
> appropriate because "In some sense DSM is a post-stratification, but in
> the sense that you are explicitly modelling how density changes as a
> function of the covariates (here ice concentration that would define
> strata), rather than defining areas over which to estimate density."
> (copied from one of Dave Miller's answers ("DSM and stratification by
> year").
>
> Thanks in advance for your confirmation/correction/answers on the above
> questions/statements.
>
> Chris

complex likelihoods using Nimble, rather than JAGS. The language is

cheers,

messages.subject_clean: Issues loading transect shapefiles with DSsim
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am working with DSsim and am trying to load a shapefile of line transects.  I created the shapefile manually in ArcGIS desktop and exported to a folder called "transects" in my R working directory.  Attempting to load transects with the following code:

new.directory <- paste(getwd(), "transects", sep = "/")
subjective.design <- make.design(transect.type = "Line", design.details = c("user specified"),  region = region, plus.sampling = FALSE, path = new.directory)

and then run a test simulation with this code:

ddf.analyses <- make.ddf.analysis.list(
  dsmodel = list(~cds(key = "hn", formula = ~1), #half-normal model
                 ~cds(key = "hr", formula = ~1)),               #hazard-rate model
  method = "ds", criteria = "AIC")

my.simulation.subjective <- make.simulation(reps = 10, single.transect.set = TRUE,
                                            region.obj = region,
                                            design.obj = subjective.design,
                                            population.description.obj = pop.description,
                                            detectability.obj = detect, ddf.analyses.list = ddf.analyses)

When I begin to plot the results and loaded transects, some transects appear in full but only small segments of others show up.

transects <- generate.transects(my.simulation.subjective)
plot(region)
plot(transects, col = 4, lwd = 3)

I've attached plots of what shows up in R, and a screen capture of what my transects are supposed to look like.

I'm thinking that the issue might have to do with the fact that I created the shapefile in ArcMap and not Distance, so I might need to delete, create, or edit the attribute table to perfectly match whatever output Distance generates.

Any ideas much appreciated,

Darryl, our software does not allow that.  It could be developed, though not sure it would be worthwhile.  Pooling robustness means that, if you use a single truncation distance, estimation should be OK – it doesn’t matter whether or not the fall-off in detectability is due to vegetation blocking the view.  I guess you may manage to get slightly improved precision by programming in different truncation distances.  All of your distances are very small, so presumably the vegetation cover is quite dense, and if you find the detection function is difficult to model adequately, then the potential gain is greater.

Steve

I'm comfortable with the idea of pooling robustness accounting for unmodelled variation in the detection function across site, but am more concerned that some cameras are placed in big clearings while others are in small clearings, so across the set of cameras, you wouldn't expect animal density to be uniform relative to distance from the camera (it would start to decline once you get to the edge of clearings; so a bit like the case when animals are attracted to observers?). If cameras were located completely at random (so you then have some really small clearings) then it probably wouldn't matter, but that's not how camera traps would typically be deployed. I was thinking that if I could use a variable right truncation distance, then that would better satisfy the assumption of uniform density relative to distance within clearings, then apply a secondary adjustment to account for what fraction of the landscape (or plot transect) is clearing vs thick veg. That's probably a better description of the issue rather than thinking about it in terms of availability, sorry.

Will re-read David's proof and keep thinking it through. Maybe I'm overthinking it, but just what to make sure that I'm not double-dipping on any adjustments.

Cheers
Darryl

PS, think this is a pretty neat way of using camera trap data, but it would be much easier if they were just set to permanently record so we didn't have to think about detection probability! ;-)

Darryl

The paper is:

Summers, R.W. and Buckland, S.T. 2011.  A first survey of the global population size and distribution of the Scottish crossbill Loxia scotica.  Bird Conservation International 21, 186-198.

In it, we estimate a ‘habitat availability’ function.  It is suitable if you have patchy suitable habitat, and your points are only placed within suitable habitat.  (Bias can be avoided by placing points in unsuitable habitat that is within detection distance of suitable habitat, but with patchy habitat, that can result in a very inefficient design.)  The triangular function pi(r) of point transect sampling can then be replaced by this estimated habitat availability function.  In the above paper, we used a lure survey for which estimation of the detection function is a little different, but the principle is the same.  The lure survey method is described in

Buckland, S.T., Summers, R.W., Borchers, D.L. and Thomas, L. 2006.  Point transect sampling with traps or lures.  J. App. Ecol. 43, 377-384.

Both papers are summarised on pp171-174 of

Buckland, S.T., Rexstad, E.A., Marques, T.A. and Oedekoven, C.S. 2015.  Distance Sampling: Methods and Applications.  Springer, New York.

Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

Thanks for your suggestions!

I am revisiting your comment because, again, I am designing a survey for an iguana on a different island (the native species on Cayman Brac, Cayman Islands) where accessibility to habitat is very limited and roads are practically necessary to move through the jagged karst terrain.

I have attached a few images of the survey area habitat and the target species if that helps paint the picture.  There is a huge bluff (i.e. cliff) the runs down the center of the island that has 200 - 500 meters of low lying areas flanking either side of it on the coast. The coastal areas are where most of the iguanas are seen and where habitat is more accessible.

Do you (or any on the group list) think that stratifying the density estimates by off-road and within a certain distance to the road (e.g. based on home range sizes of animals that may be attracted to the road) is a viable way to account for road bias for iguanas attracted to the roads? Still, the challenge will be not having enough replicates of off-road transects, likely leading to poor estimate for that region. But at least it will be more representative of the survey design.

I have read Marques et. al. (2013) on using independent location information to account for density gradients in line transects but I don't think I can implement the models described.

As a second option, I'm leaning more towards your previous suggestion; to use transects perpendicular to the road in these coastal areas where possible and then use a mix of mostly on-road or on-trail transects on the interior bluff. At least on the coast, we will be able to get a sense of how attracted the iguanas are to the road and a more precise estimate.

Any comments or suggestions would be appreciated.

All the best,

Vaughn

Hi Vaughn,

So there is a road up on the bluff, too? I think your best course of action probably depends on survey effort available to you, but it sounds like you are aware of all the relevant issues and potential sources of bias. If I am understanding this system and your species correctly, then you might hope that densities of lizards off-road are relatively low. Then you could do a mix of (relatively straightforward and quick) road transects (probably restricting sampling area to the road itself, and assuming detection rate close to 1) and perpendicular transects for off-road habitat, the latter stratified by distance to road, as you suggest. If off-road densities are relatively low then wide confidence limit on estimates from these might not be so important. Ideally, you might find that off-road densities are predicted by on-road densities in the same perpendicular transects. That might allow you to get at reasonable estimates sticking largely to road surveys.

Great photos by the way! And best of luck with your study!

Mark

messages.body_plain:
My colleagues and I are pleased to announce the publication of the following paper, which may be of interest to those of you carrying out distance sampling surveys, particularly aerial surveys.

Hansen, R. G., Pike, D., Thorgilsson, B., Gunnlaugsson, T., & Lawson, J. (2020). The Geometer: A New Device for Recording Angles in Visual Surveys. NAMMCO Scientific Publications, 11. https://doi.org/10.7557/3.5585

Abstract
The Geometer is a new handheld USB device that facilitates a relatively accurate measurement of the declination to a target with instantaneous recording of this and other data. The Geometer offers several advantages over traditional clinometers used in aerial surveys, including easier target pinpointing and tracking, more consistent angle measurements, and integration with software data collection packages. In this note we provide technical specifications for the device and its associated software, and describe a new aerial survey data collection programme that takes full advantage of the features of the Geometer. We have tested this device extensively during aerial surveys and highlight the utility of the hardware as well as ways in which the technology could be improved.

The paper is available here https://septentrio.uit.no/index.php/NAMMCOSP/article/view/5585

Best regards,
Daniel Pike.

Vaughn

A challenging problem when it comes to estimating abundance of a critically endangered species.  By definition, endangered species are rare.

Your aim should be to produce a defensible estimate.  You have discussed some of the threats to the estimate from your proposed survey.  Attempt to minimise those threats, which will likely entail more challenging field work.  A premise of design-based sampling inference is that places you survey are representative of places you do not survey.  A corollary is that if some portions of the island have zero probability of being sampled, you should not make inference about those portions of the island.

As the investigator, you choose the compromise between strength of your inference and the effort you are able to expend.

Hi Scarlett,

Great to hear you are working through the example. Regarding your question about how to choose the starting values for the MH algorithm: first you need to think about if there is a range of values that these need to fall into for the respective parameter. For example, the scale parameter of the detection function (half-normal or hazard-rate) needs to be larger than zero. After that, in theory, any values should work. However, the further this value is from what the chain will eventually converge on, the longer the chain will take to converge. To narrow down the range of options you can also think about what might make sense biologically (when dealing with biological data) and essentially have a guess at what this parameter value might be. For example, the scale parameter of a half-normal detection function will define how quickly the estimated detection probabilities drop off as distance increases. For small values, the estimated detection probabilities drop off very quickly, i.e. you have low detection probabilities at small distances, and vice versa. Here you could simply plot a detection function using a candidate starting value and see if it would make sense biologically. For example, if you plot a half-normal detection function with a scale parameter of 100 (using meters), it yields a detection probability of ~0.9 at distance 50m. Can I really expect to detect 90% of my study species at 50m? If that is too high, you can try a smaller value, and so on. You can do this for each parameter. A “quick and dirty” method to find starting values is to find the maximum likelihood parameter estimates and use these. However, remember that you should always conduct a sensitivity analysis where you test different starting values. Hope this helps!

Cornelia

Hi Scarlett,

I thought of one more thing: when you consider the starting values for the parameters associated with the covariates in the count model, you have to remember that they are modelled via the log-link function in our case. So, for example if you think about what a good starting value for the type covariate is, you will have to take this into account. The way you do this is, e.g., if you consider a starting value of 0.4 for the type covariate, you will have to consider that this value is associated with the level ‘treat’. To determine if this makes sense biologically, you have to see what effect this value would have on the response level. For this, you convert it back using exp(0.4) = 1.491825. This means that on treated fields we expect counts to be on average ~49% higher than on control fields. Here, the base-level type=control is absorbed in the intercept. Similarly, for the state covariate, one state (the base-level) is absorbed in the intercept and the others are compared with this baseline. For example, a starting value of 0.014 for state MS means that we expect counts to be ~1.4% higher in the state MS (exp(0.014) = 1.014098) than in the state of the base-level.

Cornelia

> I thought of one more thing: when you consider the starting values for the parameters associated with the covariates in the count model, you have to remember that they are modelled via the log-link function in our case. So, for example if you think about what a good starting value for the type covariate is, you will have to take this into account. The way you do this is, e.g., if you consider a starting value of 0.4 for the type covariate, you will have to consider that this value is associated with the level ‘treat’. To determine if this makes sense biologically, you have to see what effect this value would have on the response level. For this, you convert it back using exp(0.4) = 1.491825. This means that on treated fields we expect counts to be on average ~49% higher than on control fields. Here, the base-level type=control is absorbed in the intercept. Similarly, for the state covariate, one state (the base-level) is absorbed in the intercept and the others are compared with this baseline. > Great to hear you are working through the example. Regarding your question about how to choose the starting values for the MH algorithm: first you need to think about if there is a range of values that these need to fall into for the respective parameter. For example, the scale parameter of the detection function (half-normal or hazard-rate) needs to be larger than zero. After that, in theory, any values should work. However, the further this value is from what the chain will eventually converge on, the longer the chain will take to converge. To narrow down the range of options you can also think about what might make sense biologically (when dealing with biological data) and essentially have a guess at what this parameter value might be. For example, the scale parameter of a half-normal detection function will define how quickly the estimated detection probabilities drop off as distance increases. For small values, the estimated detection probabilities drop off very quickly, i.e. you have low detection probabilities at small distances, and vice versa. Here you could simply plot a detection function using a candidate starting value and see if it would make sense biologically. For example, if you plot a half-normal detection function with a scale parameter of 100 (using meters), it yields a detection probability of ~0.9 at distance 50m. Can I really expect to detect 90% of my study species at 50m? If that is too high, you can try a smaller value, and so on. You can do this for each parameter. A “quick and dirty” method to find starting values is to find the maximum likelihood parameter estimates and use these. However, remember that you should always conduct a sensitivity analysis where you test different starting values. Hope this helps!

> We are pleased to announce an update to our Distance for Windows
> software: Distance 7.3 Release 2. The new release updates the R
> packages used by the MRDS, DSM and MA analysis engines, and the
> simulation engine, with bug fixes and compatibility with R 4.0. If you
> use any of these engines, we recommend you download the new release.
> More information about what is in the updated R packages is given below.
>
> With best wishes,
>
> Len Thomas, Distance Development Group, University of St Andrews
>
> More information:
>
> The new release contains versions of the mrds, dsm, mads and DSsim
> packages, which were compiled under R 4.0.2. They implement the
> following changes:
>
> mrds 2.2.2
> ----------
>
> * fix issue in predict() when uniform key functions are used with new data.
> * new function p_dist_table() to show the distribution of estimated
> probabilities of detection. Useful for covariate models to determine
> issues with very small ps.
> * new function add_df_covar_line(), which can be used to add lines plots
> showing the detection function for a given covariate combination. Thanks
> to various members of the distance sampling mailing list for this
> suggestion.
> * plots produced by
> plot.ds/plot.rem/plot.rem.fi/plot.trial/plot.trial.fi/plot.io/plot.io.fi/plot.det.tables <http://plot.rem.fi/plot.trial/plot.trial.fi/plot.io/plot.io.fi/plot.det.tables>
> now use same defaults as R 4.0.0 ("lightgrey" bars for histograms). Some
> deprecated arguments to plot.ds were removed.
>
> mrds 2.2.1
> ----------
>
> * hessian now returned when solnp (constrained optimisation) is used to
> fit the detection function
> * Check for NA covariate values, thanks to Ana Cañadas for highlighting
> this issue.
> * enable P2 variance estimator for points
> * Corrected handling of NA covariates
> * new option se.fit for predict.ds to obtain standard errors for the
> probability of detection or ESW
> * Fixed a bug in dht when left truncation is used. Previously left
> truncation was ignored. See
> https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/mrds/issues/22 thanks to Carl
> Schwarz for finding this bug.
> * Fix bug where two objects could have a missing observer and no error
> was thrown. Thanks to Ainars Aunins for reporting this bug and Eric
> Rexstad for diagnosing.
>

> ---------
>
> * transect type (line or point) is now determined from the detection
> function rather than using the transect= argument
> * multiple detection functions are now possible, use a list() of
> fitted detection functions supplied to ddf.obj= argument to dsm().

> coming soon. Thanks to Dave Fifield and Ewan Wakefield for extensive
> testing and suggestions.

>
> dsm 2.3.0
> ---------
>
> * fixed dsm_varprop (gam.fixed.priors) for response distributions with
> fixed scale parameters. Negative binomial results before now may have
> been incorrect!
>
> dsm 2.2.18
> ----------
>

I must apologise.  There were errors in my posting from 2017.  I've revisited the subject from first principles, based upon the discussion of precision of strip transects found in Buckland et al. (2015):

The only difficult component to calculate is Eqn 6.1.  the function `varn` computes the square of this quantity (or variance of encounter rate).  Here is the code snippet that performs the calculations:

w <- 1 # strip transect with half-width=1
lvec <- rep(x = 4,times=20)
nvec <- c(0,6,2,4,7,2,1,8,3,13,15,16,10,9,7,3,2,6,3,0)

var.er <http://var.er> <- mrds:::varn(lvec=lvec, nvec=nvec, type="R2")

seD <- sqrt(var.er <http://var.er>) / 2*w  # se(D-hat) Eqn 6.3
A <- 1000 # study area size
a <- sum(lvec) * 2 * w  # covered area
# abundance estimate
abund.est <- sum(nvec) * (A/a)
seN <- seD * A  #  se(N-hat)
# Analytical normal-approximation CI
normal.ci <http://normal.ci> <- abund.est + c(-1,1)* 1.96 * seN

Don
